conclusion.justification: The report concludes that there is no firm answer to the claim, noting that while observational studies show an association, the evidence is weak, conflicted, and likely subject to reverse causation and confounding. Therefore, it treats the evidence as balanced or insufficient.
conclusion.label: hedged

report:
**Conclusion: not a firm “yes” for causing Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.** Benzodiazepines are *associated* with higher dementia rates in many observational studies, but the best synthesis judges the evidence **weak and not sufficient to establish causation**. A 2023 umbrella review of five meta-analyses (30 studies) found relative-risk estimates of **1.38–1.78**, yet rated the supporting evidence weak. [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10608561/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10608561/)

The central problem is **reverse causation (protopathic bias)** and confounding: anxiety, insomnia, depression, and subtle cognitive/behavioral changes can be early manifestations of dementia and can prompt sedative prescriptions years before diagnosis. A 2023 analysis found patterns consistent with these biases and no significant association with long-term benzodiazepine use, arguing that earlier results need reconsideration. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37312937/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37312937/)

There is genuine disagreement: a 2018 meta-analysis designed to address protopathic bias concluded the association was not *entirely* explained by it. [https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40263-018-0535-3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40263-018-0535-3) Conversely, a large Danish cohort of 235,465 people with affective disorders found no subsequent dementia association for benzodiazepines or Z-drugs. [https://www.bmj.com/content/369/bmj.m1726](https://www.bmj.com/content/369/bmj.m1726)

This uncertainty should not be read as reassurance about long-term use—especially in older adults. Benzodiazepines are well known to raise risks of **cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, and fractures**. Discuss any ongoing sedative or sleeping-pill use with the prescriber; do not stop benzodiazepines abruptly.
